title: Mending the Pen After the Sheep Are Lost
text:
Zhuang Xin, a minister of Chu, warned King Xiang that the court was in danger. The king surrounded himself with flattering favorites, lived in luxury and ignored the affairs of state, while the powerful state of Qin was watching. If this went on, Zhuang Xin said, Chu would fall.

The king was offended. He asked whether the old man had gone senile, or was trying to spread evil omens about the kingdom. Zhuang Xin replied that he was only saying what he saw, and asked permission to withdraw to the state of Zhao to wait and watch. The king let him go.

Within months, Qin attacked. The armies of Qin captured city after city, including Ying, the capital of Chu, and the king was forced to flee. In exile, he remembered the warning and sent for Zhuang Xin, asking him what could still be done.

Zhuang Xin answered with a saying. To see the hare and then turn to call the dog is not too late. To lose the sheep and then mend the pen is not too late. Chu, he said, had lost a great deal, but it still held thousands of miles of land. If the king mended his ways now, the state could still be saved.
lesson: After a first loss, do not despair and do not pretend nothing happened. Fix the weakness that caused it while you still have something left to protect.
people: Zhuang Xin, King Xiang of Chu
source: Zhanguo Ce (Strategies of the Warring States), Chu section
caveat: The dialogue comes from the Zhanguo Ce, a collection of persuasion stories whose details are not always reliable history.
